opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came from not knowing exactly what I wanted to work on yet, and being okay with that. When I started my PhD, I was in a lab where people were doing everything from computer vision to robotics, and I found that environment really stimulating. I'd see a talk or a paper in an area adjacent to mine and think, "Wait, that's actually connected to the problem I care about."

Early on I spent time on more vision-oriented problems, things like understanding scenes in a structured way, not just recognizing objects but understanding how they relate to each other. That was exciting, but over time I kept asking myself what that understanding was *for*. And the answer that kept coming back was action. If an agent understands a scene, it should be able to do something useful in it. That pulled me toward robotics and toward questions about how robots can learn and reason about long-horizon tasks.

So the motivation was partly curiosity and partly a search for the problem that felt most fundamental to me. I think early in a PhD, exploring is really valuable. You build intuition across different areas, and later those pieces come together in ways you couldn't have planned. A lot of the ideas I've worked on since came from carrying lessons from one field into another. If I had locked into one narrow direction from day one, I don't think I would have found the questions I care most about now.

r001.rationale: The response cites general curiosity and a search for meaningful problems, but does not identify curiosity about why deep learning works as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, a lot of it came from not knowing what I wanted yet. When I started my PhD, I had this broad fascination with robots that could actually do useful things in the real world, but I didn't have a clear sense of which piece of that problem was the one I should bet years on. So instead of committing early, I treated the first couple of years almost like a survey. I worked on perception-related problems, I spent time on learning from demonstration, I dabbled in task planning and more structured, symbolic approaches. Each of those felt like a different window into the same underlying question: how do you get a robot to generalize beyond the exact situations it was trained on?

The other motivation was that I was in a lab with people doing very different things, and I found it hard to ignore that. Every time I sat down with someone working on something adjacent, I'd come away thinking, "Wait, that connects to what I'm doing in a way I hadn't considered." I think if I had locked myself into one narrow direction, I would have missed the places where those threads meet, and those intersections ended up being where my most interesting work happened later.

And I'll be honest, part of it was also just managing risk. Robotics research is slow and a lot of projects don't pan out. Having a few directions going at once meant that when one stalled, I wasn't stuck. It was messier, and I probably paid for it in terms of focus early on, but it gave me a much better map of the field by the time I had to decide what my thesis was really about.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites broad interest in useful robots, uncertainty about which problem to pursue, interdisciplinary connections, and managing project risk. It does not identify curiosity about why deep learning works.

astra-6.text: Early in my PhD, I wanted to figure out which questions I really cared about. Exploring different directions helped me understand what kinds of problems I enjoyed working on and where I might be able to contribute. I didn’t have a fully formed research agenda at the beginning, so that exploration was part of developing one.

sol-6.1.text: Early in my PhD, I wanted to give myself room to figure out which questions I really cared about. I was interested in how robots could learn to do useful things, but that’s a broad goal, and there are many ways to approach it. Exploring different directions helped me understand what each approach could offer and where it fell short. It also helped me discover what kind of research I enjoyed doing. I think that exploration was valuable because it gave me a stronger basis for deciding what to focus on later.

r001.rationale: The response says he explored directions to find which robotics questions and research approaches he cared about, but does not identify curiosity about why deep learning works.
